common_name: AU Golden Sunn Hemp (Day-Neutral Seed-Producing Sunn Hemp)

planting.note: Broadcast or drill into warm soil after last frost; AU Golden flowers earlier than standard sunn hemp and can mature a viable seed crop even in the temperate Southeast.

directions: Broadcast or drill seed into warm, well-drained soil once temperatures stay reliably above 65°F, since this fast-growing tropical legume stalls in cool weather. AU Golden was bred at Auburn University from day-neutral sunn hemp germplasm specifically so growers as far north as Alabama and Georgia can save their own seed each year, unlike the older Tropic Sun cultivar, which needs short autumn days to flower and rarely sets viable seed on the mainland. Its early, abundant flowering also makes it a strong late-summer pollinator resource before it is mowed or crimped for nitrogen-rich, quickly decomposing biomass. Terminate at first bloom for maximum soil-building value, or let a portion go to seed to build up your own low-cost regional seed supply.

common_name: Joe Burton Berseem Clover (Virus- and Nematode-Resistant Multi-Cut Berseem)

planting.note: Sow in fall for a winter and spring cover; Joe Burton was bred for improved cold survival and disease resistance and can be cut repeatedly through the cool season.

directions: Broadcast inoculated seed onto a fine, fertile seedbed in fall and rake lightly for good soil contact. Joe Burton was released by the University of California from Multicut-derived germplasm and stands out among berseem clover cultivars for its resistance to root-knot nematodes, Fusarium wilt, and several common clover viruses, along with noticeably better cold tolerance than older berseem types. Its semi-erect, vigorous habit regrows quickly after mowing or grazing, supporting several cuttings for green manure or forage before it is finally terminated. Choose it over generic berseem clover on ground with a history of nematode or wilt pressure, or wherever winter temperatures dip below what standard berseem tolerates.
sources: SARE — Managing Cover Crops Profitably: Berseem Clover

common_name: Winfred Forage Brassica (Kale-Turnip Hybrid Cover Crop)

planting.note: Drill or broadcast in late summer for fall through early-winter growth; Winfred combines a kale parent's leafiness with a turnip parent's fast establishment and regrowth after cutting.

directions: Drill or broadcast seed shallowly into a firm, moist seedbed in late summer, since fine brassica seed needs only light covering to establish quickly. Winfred is a cross between forage kale and forage turnip, producing an unusually leafy plant with a modest bulb-like root, and it retains far more cold tolerance than pure forage rape, staying green and grazable even after hard freezes into the low teens. It regrows vigorously after mowing or grazing, supporting two to four cuttings across a single fall-to-winter season, and can be paired with cereal rye or clover for a mixed cover that adds nitrogen scavenging along with weed suppression. Because it holds its quality later into winter than most brassica covers, it is a good choice where a longer window of grazable or mowable green cover is wanted before spring planting.

common_name: Kinman Guar (Standard Texas Cluster Bean Cultivar)

planting.note: Sow after soil is thoroughly warm in hot, dry summer conditions; Kinman is a long-established, fine-branching Texas guar cultivar with strong disease tolerance.

directions: Direct-sow inoculated seed about 1 inch deep into hot, well-drained soil after all danger of frost has passed, since guar needs sustained heat to germinate and grow well. Kinman is one of the oldest and most widely planted commercial guar cultivars in the Texas Panhandle and South Plains, valued for its fine branching, smooth leaves, and reliable disease tolerance across a long production history. It grows through summer heat and drought with minimal irrigation while fixing nitrogen through its root nodules, making it a dependable warm-season legume cover for hot, arid soils where cowpea or soybean would struggle. Mow and incorporate at early pod fill for the best balance of biomass and easy breakdown, or let a stand fully mature to harvest guar bean seed.
sources: Texas A&M AgriLife Research and Extension

planting.note: Broadcast onto a firm seedbed in fall; Nangeela flowers and sets seed later in spring than Mt. Barker or Dalkeith, extending its living-mulch and nitrogen-fixing window.

directions: Broadcast seed over a firm, moist bed in early fall and rake lightly, since good seed-to-soil contact is essential for even establishment. Nangeela is a later-flowering subterranean clover cultivar than the classic Mt. Barker and Dalkeith types, staying green and actively fixing nitrogen further into spring before it burrows and buries its own seed pods just below the soil surface for reliable self-reseeding. Its dense, low, mat-forming growth makes it a durable living mulch under fruit trees and in orchard alleys, tolerating light foot traffic and mowing far better than upright clovers. Choose Nangeela over earlier subterranean clover cultivars where a longer spring cover window is wanted before the stand naturally dies back with rising temperatures.

planting.note: Broadcast or drill in fall on well-drained soil; Meechee matures later than Yuchi, extending flowering and nitrogen fixation deeper into late spring.

directions: Broadcast seed onto a well-prepared, well-drained bed in early fall and lightly cover, since arrowleaf clover seedlings establish slowly but grow rapidly once cool, moist weather sets in. Meechee is a later-maturing arrowleaf clover cultivar than the widely planted Yuchi, flowering and fixing nitrogen further into late spring before it finally sets seed, which lengthens the pollinator forage and cover window in a mixed winter-annual planting. Its tall, upright growth and arrow-shaped leaves distinguish it in the field from crimson or white clover stands, and it reseeds readily on well-drained soils when allowed to flower before termination. Pair it with an earlier arrowleaf cultivar or crimson clover in a blend to spread bloom time and grazing or green-manure availability across more of the spring.
sources: Auburn University Alabama Agricultural Experiment Station

common_name: Joelle Winter Camelina (Cold-Hardy Cash Cover Crop Oilseed)

planting.note: Drill in early fall so plants reach a small rosette before hard freezes; Joelle requires winter cold (vernalization) to bolt and flower the following spring.

directions: Drill seed shallowly into a firm, fine seedbed in early fall, giving plants enough time to form a low rosette before hard frost, since Joelle is a true winter-annual type that needs a period of cold exposure before it will bolt and flower the following spring. Bred in France and now widely studied and grown across the Midwest and northern Plains, Joelle is the most extensively used winter camelina cultivar for relay or double cropping, overwintering as a rosette, then flowering and setting oil-rich seed early enough in summer to be harvested ahead of a full-season soybean or other warm-season crop planted into the same field. Its deep, fibrous root system and dense fall-to-spring canopy scavenge residual soil nitrogen and outcompete winter weeds, while its oilseed is a genuine harvestable cash crop rather than a pure green manure. Because it depends on real winter chill to flower reliably, it performs best in cold-winter regions and is not a good fit for mild-winter areas that lack sufficient vernalization.
